questions.q:
Consider the statements about triangles and their construction.
Statement 1: The vertices of a triangle can be written in any order, so triangle YZX and triangle XYZ are the same triangle.
Statement 2: Angle A of triangle ABC means the angle at the vertex A.
Statement 3: An equilateral triangle can be constructed with a compass only if its side is a whole number of centimetres.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the compass construction of an equilateral triangle on base AB, both arcs have a radius equal to AB.
Reason (R): Only then are all three sides AB, AC and BC equal, which an equilateral triangle needs.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match the terms in Column I with their meanings in Column II.
Column I: 1. Vertex  2. Side  3. Angle B of triangle ABC  4. Equilateral triangle
Column II: A. The angle at the corner B  B. A corner point of the triangle  C. A line segment joining two vertices  D. A triangle with all three sides of equal length
(a) Write the steps, with the compass settings, to construct an equilateral triangle of side 5.5 cm. (b) Explain why the third vertex you mark is exactly 5.5 cm from both ends of the base.
questions.a: (a) Draw AB = 5.5 cm. With the compass opened to 5.5 cm, draw an arc from A and then an arc from B so that they cross at C. Join AC and BC. (b) C lies on the arc centred at A, so AC = 5.5 cm, and on the arc centred at B, so BC = 5.5 cm.
s: Part (a): base 5.5 cm, two arcs of radius 5.5 cm from the two ends, join the crossing point
Part (b): the crossing point lies on both arcs, so it is a radius away from each centre

questions.q: (a) Write all six possible names of the triangle whose vertices are P, Q and R. (b) Write the angle at Q using three letters in both possible ways.
questions.a: (a) PQR, PRQ, QPR, QRP, RPQ, RQP. (b) angle PQR and angle RQP (the vertex Q stays in the middle).
s: Part (a): lists all six orderings of P, Q, R
Part (b): angle PQR and angle RQP with Q in the middle

questions.q: O is the centre of a circle of radius 3 cm, and P and Q are two points on the circle (not in line with O, and PQ is not 3 cm). (a) What are the lengths of OP and OQ? (b) What kind of triangle is OPQ by its sides, and why?
questions.a: (a) OP = OQ = 3 cm, since both are radii. (b) Triangle OPQ is isosceles because two of its sides, OP and OQ, are equal.
s: Part (a): both radii equal 3 cm
Part (b): names it isosceles because two sides are equal

questions.q: Three points K, L and M lie on one straight line, with L between K and M, KL = 3 cm and LM = 4 cm. (a) Find KM. (b) Can K, L and M be the vertices of a triangle? Say what the 'triangle' KLM looks like.
questions.a: (a) KM = 3 + 4 = 7 cm. (b) No. With the three points on a line, the 'sides' KL and LM lie along KM, so the figure is just a straight line segment and encloses no region; there is no triangle.
s: Part (a): KM = 7 cm
Part (b): no triangle, the figure collapses to a straight segment

questions.q: Write the angles of triangle ABC at the vertices A, B and C using three letters each, and say why the order of the letters in a triangle's name does not matter but the middle letter in an angle's name does.
questions.a: Angle A = angle CAB, angle B = angle ABC, angle C = angle BCA. A triangle's name only lists its three vertices, in any order; an angle's middle letter tells which vertex the angle is at.
s: Names the three angles as CAB, ABC and BCA
Explains that the middle letter marks the vertex of the angle while the triangle name is just its vertices

questions.q: Tara says: 'On AB = 4 cm, my two 4 cm arcs cross above AB at C. The crossing point below AB is not 4 cm from both A and B, so it cannot give an equilateral triangle on AB.' Do you agree? Give the reason.
questions.a: No. The two circles of radius 4 cm centred at A and B cut each other at two points, and each is 4 cm from A and 4 cm from B. The lower point therefore gives AC = BC = AB = 4 cm, an equilateral triangle on the other side of AB.
s: Verdict that Tara is wrong
Says the arcs meet at two points, one on each side of AB
Shows the lower point is also 4 cm from A and B, so its triangle is equilateral

questions.q: A student's rough notes read: 'Draw AB = 6.5 cm. Set the compass to 6.5 cm. Draw an arc from A and an arc from B so they cross at C. Join AC and BC.' (a) Name the triangle by its sides and give all three side lengths. (b) Write the question the student was answering.
questions.a: (a) Equilateral: AB = AC = BC = 6.5 cm. (b) 'Construct an equilateral triangle of side 6.5 cm.'
s: Part (a): names it equilateral
Part (a): gives all three sides as 6.5 cm, with C on both arcs
Part (b): the question set was an equilateral triangle of side 6.5 cm

questions.q: A student says the equilateral triangle can be drawn with a marked ruler alone, so the compass is just a luxury. Explain how it can be done with the ruler only, what goes wrong, and how the compass fixes it.
questions.a: With only a ruler, draw AB and mark C with AC equal to the side; BC may not equal the side, so C must be moved again and again until BC is also correct. The compass draws arcs from both ends at once, and where they cross C is the right distance from A and B immediately, with no trials.
s: Describes the ruler method: mark C with AC equal to the side
Says BC may not come out right so many trials are needed
Says the two arcs meet at C and fix both distances at once

questions.q: Write the full construction of an isosceles triangle ABC in which the base AB = 5 cm and AC = BC = 6 cm. (a) Give the steps with compass settings. (b) Explain why the crossing point is the correct third vertex. (c) Name the three angles of the triangle using three letters.
questions.a: (a) Draw AB = 5 cm. With the compass at 6 cm, draw an arc from A and another from B so that they cross at C. Join AC and BC. (b) C lies on both arcs, so AC = 6 cm and BC = 6 cm, which makes the triangle isosceles. (c) Angle CAB, angle ABC and angle BCA.
s: Part (a): draws the 5 cm base
Part (a): two 6 cm arcs from the ends and joins the crossing point to get AC and BC
Part (b): crossing point is on both arcs so both sides are 6 cm
Part (c): names angles CAB, ABC and BCA

questions.q: Two circles of the same radius 5 cm have centres A and B, and AB = 5 cm. They cross at two points, C and D. (a) Why is triangle ABC equilateral? (b) Why is triangle ABD equilateral? (c) Name another triangle with an equal pair of sides, give the pair and the kind of triangle it is.
questions.a: (a) AC and BC are radii of the two circles, each 5 cm, and AB = 5 cm, so all three sides are 5 cm. (b) In the same way AD = BD = 5 cm = AB. (c) Triangle ACD has AC = AD = 5 cm (both radii of the circle centred at A), so it is isosceles.
s: Part (a): AC = BC = AB = 5 cm so equilateral
Part (b): AD = BD = AB = 5 cm so equilateral
Part (c): triangle ACD with AC = AD radii of one circle, isosceles

questions.q:
The craft club of a school in Madurai must cut 12 equilateral card flags of side 8 cm. Ananya marks the third vertex with a ruler only: she draws AB = 8 cm, marks C with AC = 8 cm and then checks BC, needing about 6 tries of 30 seconds each for every flag. Using a compass takes 90 seconds per flag. The 12 flags can be shared by 3 groups of 4 flags each. The club owns one ruler per group but only one compass, and passing the compass from one group to the next costs 5 minutes each time.
(a) State the radius of the arcs drawn from A and from B for one flag, and what you draw first.
(b) Explain why the crossing point of the arcs is exactly 8 cm from both A and B.
(c) Find the total time in minutes if the three groups work at the same time with rulers, and the total time if the one compass is used by group 1, then group 2, then group 3 (two hand-overs).
(d) Which method should the club choose for finishing quickly, and what else would you weigh before deciding?
questions.a: (a) Radius 8 cm for both arcs; first the base AB = 8 cm. (b) The point lies on the arc centred at A and on the arc centred at B, so it is 8 cm from each. (c) Ruler: each group makes 4 flags x 6 x 30 s = 720 s = 12 minutes, in parallel. Compass: 12 x 90 s = 18 minutes + 2 x 5 = 10 minutes = 28 minutes. (d) The rulers finish in 12 minutes against 28, so on time alone the club should use rulers in parallel; against that, ruler-made flags may not have BC exactly 8 cm, so a club that values accuracy over time might still choose the compass for a few model flags.
s: Part (a): radius 8 cm, base drawn first
Part (b): crossing point lies on both arcs
Part (c): 12 minutes for rulers and 28 minutes for the shared compass
Part (d): chooses rulers in parallel on time (12 against 28) and names accuracy of the third side as the trade-off

questions.q:
A garden designer in Jaipur plans a circular pond with centre O and radius 6 m. Two lamp posts P and Q stand on the edge of the pond, and a cable is laid along OP, PQ and QO at ₹450 per metre. The committee has a budget of ₹8,600 and wants the stretch PQ to be at least 7 m so that a bench fits there.
(a) If PQ = 8 m, what kind of triangle by its sides is OPQ, and why?
(b) If PQ = 6 m, what kind of triangle is OPQ?
(c) Find the cable cost when PQ = 6 m and when PQ = 8 m.
(d) The designer can choose PQ = 6, 7 or 8 m. Which choice meets both the budget and the bench requirement? Show the cost.
questions.a: (a) OP = OQ = 6 m (radii), so OPQ is isosceles. (b) All three sides are 6 m, so OPQ is equilateral. (c) PQ = 6: perimeter 18 m, cost 18 x 450 = ₹8,100. PQ = 8: perimeter 20 m, cost ₹9,000. (d) PQ = 6 fails the 7 m bench; PQ = 8 costs ₹9,000, over ₹8,600; PQ = 7 m gives perimeter 19 m and cost 19 x 450 = ₹8,550, within budget and at least 7 m, so choose 7 m.
s: Part (a): OP and OQ are radii so isosceles
Part (b): all sides 6 m so equilateral
Part (c): costs of ₹8,100 and ₹9,000
Part (d): chooses PQ = 7 m with cost ₹8,550 against both constraints

questions.a: an isosceles triangle with AC = BC = 4 cm

questions.q:
Read the statements about constructing a triangle when its three sides are given.
Statement 1: The longest of the three given lengths must always be taken as the base.
Statement 2: Drawing the full circles is not necessary; arcs that cross are enough to find the third vertex.
Statement 3: A triangle with sides 1 cm, 5 cm and 5 cm can be constructed in the same way.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Any one of the three given lengths may be chosen as the base in the construction of a triangle from its sides.
Reason (R): The two arcs drawn from the ends of the base always have the same radius.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: A student draws AB = 5 cm, then an arc of radius 6 cm from A and an arc of radius 3 cm from B, which cross at C. The sides of triangle ABC are
questions.a: AB = 5 cm, AC = 6 cm, BC = 3 cm
o: AB = 5 cm, AC = 6 cm, BC = 3 cm
AB = 5 cm, AC = 3 cm, BC = 6 cm
AB = 5 cm, AC = 6 cm, BC = 6 cm
AB = 6 cm, AC = 5 cm, BC = 3 cm

questions.q: (a) Write the steps to construct triangle PQR with PQ = 5 cm, QR = 6 cm and PR = 7 cm, taking PQ as the base. (b) State why the point R you mark is 7 cm from P and 6 cm from Q.
questions.a: (a) Draw PQ = 5 cm. From P draw an arc of radius 7 cm and from Q an arc of radius 6 cm so that they cross at R. Join PR and QR. (b) R lies on the arc centred at P (radius 7 cm) and on the arc centred at Q (radius 6 cm).
s: Part (a): base 5 cm, arcs of 7 cm from P and 6 cm from Q, joins R
Part (b): R lies on both arcs so it is a radius from each centre

questions.q: A triangle has sides 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm. (a) If the 6 cm side is the base, what are the two arc radii? (b) If a 4 cm side is the base, what are the two arc radii?
questions.a: (a) Base 6 cm; arcs of 4 cm from each end. (b) Base 4 cm; one arc of 4 cm and one arc of 6 cm from the two ends.
s: Part (a): two arcs of 4 cm from the ends of the 6 cm base
Part (b): arcs of 4 cm and 6 cm from the ends of a 4 cm base

questions.q: Mira wants a triangle with sides 6 cm, 7 cm and 9 cm. She draws AB = 6 cm and then, from A, an arc of radius 7 cm and another arc of radius 9 cm. (a) What is her mistake? (b) How should the second arc be drawn so that the crossing point is the third vertex?
questions.a: (a) Both arcs are centred at A, so they never cross at a point that is correct for the other end of the base. (b) The 9 cm arc should be centred at B, so that C is 7 cm from A and 9 cm from B (or the 7 cm arc at B and 9 cm at A).
s: Part (a): both arcs from the same end A
Part (b): the second arc is drawn from B so the crossing point is 7 cm from A and 9 cm from B

questions.q: A triangle has sides 2 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm. (a) Taking a 6 cm side as base, give the two arc radii. (b) Name the triangle by its sides and say which two sides are equal.
questions.a: (a) Base AB = 6 cm; arc of radius 6 cm from A and arc of radius 2 cm from B. (b) AB = AC = 6 cm, so it is isosceles.
s: Part (a): radii 6 cm and 2 cm
Part (b): isosceles with the two 6 cm sides equal

questions.q: Differentiate between an isosceles and a scalene triangle, giving the side lengths of one example of each from 4 cm, 4 cm, 6 cm and 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm.
questions.a: An isosceles triangle has two sides of equal length (4, 4, 6); a scalene triangle has all three sides different (3, 4, 5).
s: Isosceles: two equal sides with the example 4, 4, 6
Scalene: three different sides with the example 3, 4, 5

questions.q: Sana says: 'On AB = 6 cm for a triangle with sides 6, 4 and 5 cm, I get the required sides whether I draw the 4 cm arc from A and the 5 cm arc from B, or the 5 cm arc from A and the 4 cm arc from B. And C ends up at the same place both times.' Is she right on both counts? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. Either way C is 4 cm from one end and 5 cm from the other, so the sides are 6, 4 and 5 cm. But the two crossing points are different (mirror positions about the middle of AB), so C is not at the same place.
s: Verdict: right about the sides, wrong about the place
Reason: C is the right distance from each end in both cases
Says the two arrangements give different crossing points, so C is not at the same place

questions.q: An examiner's answer sheet shows that on a base AB = 8 cm, arcs of radius 5 cm were drawn from A and from B and crossed at C. Write the question the examiner set, and name the triangle by its sides.
questions.a: Question: construct a triangle with sides 8 cm, 5 cm and 5 cm. AC = BC = 5 cm, so the triangle is isosceles.
s: Sides given as 8 cm, 5 cm and 5 cm
Notes the arcs from both ends have radius equal to the other two sides
Names it isosceles because AC = BC

questions.q: Write the steps to construct a triangle with sides 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm, taking the 6 cm side as base, and say what you would measure at the end to check your work.
questions.a: Draw AB = 6 cm. With compass at 4 cm, draw an arc from A and another from B crossing at C. Join AC and BC. Check by measuring AC and BC: both should be 4 cm.
s: Draws base AB = 6 cm
Draws two arcs of 4 cm from A and B and joins the crossing point
Checks AC and BC are each 4 cm

questions.q: (a) Construct (write the steps for) a triangle with sides 7 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm, taking the 7 cm side as base. (b) Now write the two arc radii if you take the 4 cm side as the base. (c) Explain what you expect about the side lengths of the two triangles.
questions.a: (a) Draw AB = 7 cm; arc of 5 cm from A and arc of 4 cm from B cross at C; join AC and BC. (b) Base 4 cm; arcs of 7 cm and 5 cm from its ends. (c) Both triangles have sides 7 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm: the choice of base only changes how the triangle is drawn, not its sides.
s: Part (a): base 7 cm and the arcs of 5 cm and 4 cm
Part (a): joins the crossing point to both ends
Part (b): arcs of 7 cm and 5 cm on a 4 cm base
Part (c): same side lengths whichever base is chosen

questions.q: A triangle has sides 6 cm, 6 cm and 5 cm. (a) What kind of triangle is it by sides? (b) Write the steps to construct it with the 5 cm side as base. (c) The two arcs cross at two points, one above the base and one below. Explain why either point gives a correct triangle.
questions.a: (a) Isosceles, two sides are 6 cm. (b) Draw AB = 5 cm; arcs of 6 cm from A and from B; join A and B to the crossing point C. (c) Each crossing point lies on both circles, so it is 6 cm from A and 6 cm from B; the triangle above and the one below the base have the same sides.
s: Part (a): isosceles
Part (b): 5 cm base and two arcs of 6 cm
Part (c): both crossing points are 6 cm from A and B, so both work

questions.q:
Mr Rathore, a carpenter in Jodhpur, makes triangular corner shelves. Shelf X has sides 30 cm, 40 cm and 50 cm. Shelf Y has sides 30 cm, 30 cm and 40 cm. He first draws each shelf on paper at a scale of 1 cm for every 10 cm. His compass can open to at most 4.5 cm.
(a) What are the sides of the drawing of shelf X?
(b) If the 4 cm side of the drawing of X is taken as the base, which two arc radii are needed?
(c) What kind of triangle is shelf Y by its sides, and which radii are needed if its 4 cm side is the base?
(d) Which side of shelf X should he take as base so that his compass can be used, and why?
questions.a: (a) 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm. (b) 3 cm and 5 cm. (c) Isosceles; arcs of 3 cm and 3 cm. (d) With base 5 cm the arcs are 3 cm and 4 cm, both within 4.5 cm; with base 4 cm he needs 5 cm, and with base 3 cm he needs 4 cm and 5 cm, so he must take the 5 cm side as base.
s: Part (a): 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm
Part (b): arcs of 3 cm and 5 cm
Part (c): isosceles with radii 3 cm and 3 cm
Part (d): chooses the 5 cm base because the other arcs, 3 cm and 4 cm, fit the compass

questions.q:
Three friends fix poles A, B and C in a field and join them with rope at ₹35 per metre. They have three layouts: Layout 1 has sides 8 m, 6 m and 7 m; Layout 2 has sides 8 m, 5 m and 5 m; Layout 3 has sides 8 m, 4 m and 5 m. On their plan, 1 cm stands for 1 m. The compass they have opens only up to 6.5 cm, and the budget is ₹700. They also want two ropes of equal length so that one pre-cut length can serve twice.
(a) Name each layout's triangle by its sides.
(b) For Layout 2, taking 8 m as the base, what are the two arc radii on the plan?
(c) Which layout can the compass not draw, and why?
(d) Which layout should they choose when all three conditions (compass, budget, two equal ropes) matter? Give the cost, and say what they give up compared with the cheapest drawable layout.
questions.a: (a) Layout 1 scalene, Layout 2 isosceles, Layout 3 scalene. (b) 5 cm and 5 cm. (c) Layout 1: whichever side is the base, an arc of 7 cm or 8 cm is needed, more than 6.5 cm. (d) Layout 2: drawable, ₹630 (under ₹700) and has two equal 5 m ropes. Layout 3 costs 17 x 35 = ₹595, which is ₹35 cheaper, but it has no equal ropes; so they pay ₹35 more for the equal pair.
s: Part (a): scalene, isosceles, scalene
Part (b): radii 5 cm and 5 cm
Part (c): Layout 1 needs an arc of 7 cm or more
Part (d): Layout 2 at ₹630, and the ₹35 extra against Layout 3 is the price of the equal ropes

questions.a: Impossible: the direct 30 m is more than 12 + 15 = 27 m

questions.q:
Read the statements about the triangle inequality.
Statement 1: If the longest of three lengths is less than the sum of the other two, a triangle with those sides exists.
Statement 2: All three comparisons must always be made before we can say a triangle exists.
Statement 3: The lengths 3 cm, 3 cm and 7 cm do not satisfy the triangle inequality.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

Assertion (A): The lengths 5 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm can be the sides of a triangle.
Reason (R): A triangle whose sides are 5 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm has two equal sides, so it is isosceles.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

Match each set of lengths in Column I with what happens when the circles are drawn on the longest side in Column II.
Column I: 1. 3, 4, 8  2. 3, 5, 8  3. 4, 5, 8  4. 8, 8, 8

(a) Test whether 7 cm, 9 cm and 17 cm can be the sides of a triangle. (b) The 17 cm length is replaced by a whole number of centimetres so that a triangle becomes possible. What is the greatest whole number that works?
questions.a: (a) 7 + 9 = 16, which is less than 17, so no triangle. (b) The new length must be less than 16, so the greatest whole number is 15 (7, 9, 15 works since 7 + 9 = 16 > 15).
s: Part (a): 7 + 9 = 16 is less than 17, so no triangle
Part (b): new length must be less than 16, so 15

questions.q: Towns A, B and C are joined by straight roads. A to B is 8 km, A to C is 3 km and C to B is 4 km. (a) Compare the direct road A to B with the route through C. (b) What does the result say about A, B and C forming a triangle?
questions.a: (a) Direct 8 km is longer than 3 + 4 = 7 km via C. (b) The direct path should be the shortest, so these distances cannot belong to a triangle; no triangle exists with sides 3, 4 and 8.
s: Part (a): 8 km direct against 7 km via C
Part (b): the direct path is longer than the roundabout path, so no triangle

questions.q: Make the three comparisons for the lengths 8 cm, 11 cm and 18 cm and say whether a triangle exists.
questions.a: 8 < 11 + 18 = 29; 11 < 8 + 18 = 26; 18 < 8 + 11 = 19. All three hold, so a triangle exists.
s: Makes the three comparisons correctly (29, 26, 19)
Concludes a triangle exists because all three hold

questions.q: Two sides of a triangle are 4 cm and 9 cm. (a) Between which two numbers must the third side lie? (b) How many whole-number lengths are possible for it?
questions.a: (a) The third side must be more than 9 - 4 = 5 cm and less than 9 + 4 = 13 cm. (b) Whole numbers 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12: seven lengths.
s: Part (a): between 5 cm and 13 cm
Part (b): the seven whole numbers 6 to 12

questions.q: Why is it enough to compare only the longest length with the sum of the other two when we test the triangle inequality?
questions.a: Each of the other two lengths is no longer than the longest, so it is automatically less than the longest plus the remaining length; only the longest can fail.
s: Says the shorter lengths are not longer than the longest
Concludes the other two comparisons are automatically true

questions.q: Isha says: 'With two sides fixed at 6 cm and 6 cm, every third side x cm from 0 up to and including 12 gives a triangle.' Do you agree? Test both ends and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. At x = 12 we get 6 + 6 = 12, the circles touch and there is no triangle. At x = 0 there is no side at all. The third side must satisfy 0 < x < 12.
s: Tests the upper end: x = 12 gives 6 + 6 = 12, so the circles only touch
Tests the lower end: x = 0 is not a length
Gives the verdict: wrong, the true range is x greater than 0 and less than 12

questions.q: Show, without constructing it, that no triangle has sides 14 cm, 22 cm and 45 cm.
questions.a: The longest side is 45 cm. The other two add to 14 + 22 = 36 cm, which is less than 45 cm. The direct path of 45 cm would be longer than the roundabout path of 36 cm, which is absurd, so no triangle exists.
s: Identifies 45 cm as the longest and adds the other two to get 36 cm
Notes 36 is less than 45
Concludes the direct path would be longer than the roundabout path so no triangle

questions.q: On a 10 cm base, the radii of the two circles are the two smaller lengths. Write one set of three lengths for which the circles touch and one for which they do not meet, and give the reason for each.
questions.a: Touch: for example 4, 6, 10, because 4 + 6 = 10. Do not meet: for example 3, 4, 10, because 3 + 4 = 7, which is less than 10. Neither set gives a triangle.
s: A valid touching set such as 4, 6, 10 with sum equal to the longest
A valid non-meeting set such as 3, 4, 10 with sum less than the longest
States that neither gives a triangle

questions.q: Two sides of a triangle are 5 cm and 12 cm and the third side is x cm. (a) Write the condition that 12 is less than the sum of the other two. (b) Write the condition that x is less than the sum of 5 and 12. (c) State the range of x. (d) Explain why x = 7 and x = 17 do not give triangles.
questions.a: (a) 12 < 5 + x, so x > 7. (b) x < 5 + 12 = 17. (c) 7 < x < 17. (d) At x = 7, 5 + 7 = 12, so the circles touch; at x = 17, 5 + 12 = 17, so the longest side equals the sum of the others; neither is strictly less, so no triangle.
s: Part (a): x is more than 7
Part (b): x is less than 17
Part (c): the range 7 to 17
Part (d): at 7 and 17 the sums equal the longest side, giving no triangle

questions.q: Does an equilateral triangle exist for every side length? (a) Test sides 2.5 m, 2.5 m, 2.5 m. (b) For a side s, write the condition and say why it always holds. (c) Say what the two circles of radius s on a base of length s do.
questions.a: (a) 2.5 < 2.5 + 2.5 = 5, so it exists. (b) For any s the condition is s < s + s = 2s, which is true for every positive s, so an equilateral triangle exists for every side length. (c) The circles of radius s with centres s apart cross at two points, and either point gives the third vertex.
s: Part (a): 2.5 < 5 so it exists
Part (b): s < 2s holds for every positive s
Part (c): the circles cross at two points, so a third vertex exists

questions.q:
At a school in Pune the main gate G, library L and canteen C are to be the corners of a triangular garden. A surveyor measures GL = 60 m, LC = 50 m and the direct path GC = 115 m. A second look shows that any one of the three tape readings could be wrong by up to 6 m, but no more. Re-measuring costs ₹4 for every metre of path measured, and the school will re-measure just one path first.
(a) Compare the route from G to C through L with the direct path.
(b) If the other two readings are right, in what range must each single reading lie for a triangle to exist?
(c) With an error of at most 6 m, which of the three readings could be the faulty one?
(d) Which path should be re-measured first? Give the three costs and your choice with a reason.
questions.a: (a) Via L: 60 + 50 = 110 m, less than the direct 115 m, so the readings cannot be right. (b) GC must be less than 110 m (and more than 10 m); GL must be more than 65 m (and less than 165 m); LC must be more than 55 m (and less than 175 m). (c) All three: GC could really be 109 m, GL 66 m or LC 56 m, each within 6 m of the reading. (d) Re-measuring GC costs 115 x 4 = ₹460, GL costs ₹240 and LC costs ₹200. Each reading is equally likely to be the faulty one, so start with the cheapest, LC at ₹200; if the three readings still fail the check, re-measure the next.
s: Part (a): 110 m via L against 115 m direct, so the readings fail
Part (b): GC < 110, GL > 65, LC > 55
Part (c): each of the three could be the faulty reading within 6 m
Part (d): costs 460, 240, 200 and a reasoned choice of LC first

questions.q:
In a craft class four groups each get three straws and must form a triangle. Group A has 8 cm, 9 cm and 15 cm. Group B has 7 cm, 11 cm and 18 cm. Group C has 6 cm, 10 cm and 12 cm. Group D has 5 cm, 5 cm and 10 cm. The teacher keeps these spare straws: 3 cm, 9 cm, 10 cm and 12 cm.
(a) Which groups can form a triangle?
(b) For each group that cannot, name what the circles on its longest side do.
(c) Group D keeps its two 5 cm straws and swaps only the 10 cm straw. Between which two lengths must the new straw lie?
(d) Which spare straw should Group D take if it wants the triangle with the largest perimeter? Give the perimeter.
questions.a: (a) A (8 + 9 = 17 > 15) and C (6 + 10 = 16 > 12). (b) B: 7 + 11 = 18, so the circles touch; D: 5 + 5 = 10, so they touch. (c) More than 0 cm and less than 10 cm. (d) 3 cm and 9 cm work; 10 cm and 12 cm do not. The 9 cm straw gives 5 + 5 + 9 = 19 cm, larger than 5 + 5 + 3 = 13 cm, so take the 9 cm straw.
s: Part (a): groups A and C
Part (b): B and D each have circles that touch because the two smaller lengths add to the longest
Part (c): the new straw is less than 10 cm
Part (d): picks the 9 cm straw with perimeter 19 cm after ruling out 10 and 12

questions.q:

questions.q: (a) Write the steps to construct triangle PQR with PQ = 6 cm, PR = 3.5 cm and angle P = 70°. (b) Name the two sides between which the angle P lies.
questions.a: (a) Draw PQ = 6 cm. At P construct an angle of 70°. On the new arm mark R with PR = 3.5 cm. Join QR. (b) PQ and PR.

questions.q: Two angles of a triangle are 62° and 85°, with an included side of 5 cm. (a) Does a triangle exist? Show the check. (b) If the included side is changed to 9 cm, does your answer change, and what is the third angle?
questions.a: (a) 62 + 85 = 147, which is less than 180, so a triangle exists. (b) No change: the side length does not affect existence or the third angle, which is 180 - 147 = 33°.
s: Part (a): the sum 147 is less than 180 so it exists
Part (b): the length plays no part and the third angle is 33°

questions.q: State the rule that tells us whether a triangle exists for two given angles, and apply it to 75° and 110°.
questions.a: A triangle exists when the sum of the two angles is less than 180°; if the sum is 180 or more it does not. 75 + 110 = 185, so no triangle exists.
s: States the rule with the sum less than 180°
Applies it: 185 is not less than 180 so no triangle

questions.q: On a base AB, the angle at A is 55° and the line from B makes an angle B with AB on the same side of AB as the line from A. (a) What is the smallest angle B for which the two lines do not meet (the line from B is then parallel to the line from A)? (b) State the angles B for which a triangle does exist.
questions.a: (a) AB is a transversal and the interior angles on the same side add to 180°, so angle B = 180° - 55° = 125°. (b) Any angle B less than 125°.
s: Part (a): angle B = 125°
Part (b): triangle exists for angle B less than 125°

questions.q: For two angles and the included side, the third vertex is the point where the arms drawn from the two ends of the base meet. (a) Why must both angles be drawn on the same side of the base? (b) What do you get if the 125° and 40° arms are drawn on opposite sides of the base?
questions.a: (a) If they are on opposite sides, one arm goes up and the other goes down, so they can never cross. (b) No triangle: the arms diverge from each other and meet nowhere.
s: Part (a): arms on opposite sides cannot cross
Part (b): the 125° and 40° arms on opposite sides give no meeting point, so no triangle

questions.q: Saanvi says: 'With two sides of 3 cm and 4 cm, any included angle from 1° to 179° gives a triangle, but an angle of 180° or 0° does not.' Do you agree? Give the reason for each end.
questions.a: She is right. For any included angle between 0° and 180°, the arm leaves the base at an angle and the point on it 4 cm from the vertex, joined to the other end, gives a triangle. At 180° the arm continues the base in a straight line, and at 0° it lies along the base, so the three points are on one line and there is no triangle.
s: Verdict that she is right
Reason for the range: the arm leaves the base at an angle, so joining the ends gives a triangle
Reason for the ends: at 0° or 180° the three points lie on a line

questions.q: Show that there is no triangle with angles 125° and 70° on a base of any length. Use the line through A parallel to the line from B.
questions.a: At A the angle is 125°, so the parallel line from B would make an angle of 180 - 125 = 55° at B. The angle at B is 70°, which is 55° or more, so the line from B leans away more than the parallel line and never meets the line from A. The sum 125 + 70 = 195 is more than 180.
s: Finds the angle of the parallel line, 55°
Shows 70° is not less than 55° so the lines do not meet
Confirms with the sum 195 which is not less than 180

questions.q: Write one set of two angles and an included side that has an obtuse angle but still gives a triangle, and one set that does not. Give the check for each.
questions.a: Exists: 120° and 40° with a 6 cm included side, since 120 + 40 = 160, which is less than 180. Does not exist: 120° and 60° with a 6 cm side, since the sum is exactly 180.
s: A valid set with an obtuse angle and sum below 180, such as 120 and 40
A set with sum 180 or more, such as 120 and 60

questions.q: Construct triangle XYZ with XY = 6.5 cm, angle X = 60° and angle Y = 50°. (a) Give the steps. (b) Explain why the two arms meet. (c) Find angle Z using the angle sum. (d) By its angles, what kind of triangle is it?
questions.a: (a) Draw XY = 6.5 cm; draw 60° at X and 50° at Y on the same side; the arms meet at Z. (b) 60 + 50 = 110, which is less than 180, so the arms meet. (c) Angle Z = 180 - 110 = 70°. (d) All three angles (60, 50, 70) are acute, so it is acute-angled.

Part (b): the sum 110 is less than 180
Part (c): angle Z is 70°
Part (d): acute-angled

questions.q: Rahul has two sets of data. Set 1: sides 5 cm and 8 cm with an included angle of 40°. Set 2: angle A = 65°, angle B = 115° and AB = 5 cm. (a) Can a triangle be drawn from Set 1? (b) Explain why Set 2 gives no triangle. (c) For angle A = 65°, give the range of angle B for which a triangle exists. (d) Would a longer AB help in Set 2?
questions.a: (a) Yes, an included angle less than 180° always gives a triangle. (b) 65 + 115 = 180, so the line from B is parallel to the line from A and they never meet. (c) Angle B less than 115°. (d) No; the length of AB plays no part.
s: Part (a): yes, angle below 180°
Part (b): the sum is 180, so the lines are parallel
Part (c): angle B less than 115°
Part (d): no, AB length does not matter

questions.q:
In a science class every group draws a triangle with angles 50° and 60° on a different included side, then measures the third angle with a protractor. Group 1 used 4 cm and measured 71°; Group 2 used 6 cm and measured 69°; Group 3 used 8 cm and measured 70°; Group 4 used 10 cm and measured 79°.
(a) Find the third angle that should result without any construction.
(b) Which groups are within 1 degree of it?
(c) Does the data suggest the included side changes the third angle? Explain.
(d) What should the teacher tell Group 4: accept the reading or construct again? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 180 - 50 - 60 = 70°. (b) Groups 1, 2 and 3. (c) No: the sides 4, 6 and 8 cm give nearly the same angle, so the side has no real effect. (d) Construct and measure again: 79° is 9° away, far more than the 1 degree scatter of the others, so it is probably a drawing or reading mistake rather than an effect of the 10 cm side.
s: Part (a): third angle is 70°
Part (b): groups 1, 2 and 3
Part (c): the side length does not change the angle, shown by the three near-equal readings
Part (d): redo group 4 since 9° off is much more than the scatter in the others

questions.q:
Two surveyors stand at points A and B, 80 m apart on a straight river bank, and both sight a tree T on the far side. The surveyor at A reads angle TAB = 48°. The surveyor at B has two possible readings for angle TBA: 125° or 135°. The village will accept a survey only if the angle at the tree, angle ATB, is at least 20°.
(a) What is the greatest whole-number reading of angle TBA that allows a triangle to exist?
(b) Can the reading 135° be correct? Why?
(c) For the reading 125°, find angle ATB.
(d) Should the village accept either reading? Give your decision and a reason.
questions.a: (a) Angle B must be less than 180 - 48 = 132°, so 131°. (b) No: 48 + 135 = 183, which is 180 or more, so the lines from A and B never meet. (c) 180 - 48 - 125 = 7°. (d) Neither: 135° is impossible and with 125° the angle at T is only 7°, below 20°. B should measure again.
s: Part (a): 131°
Part (b): 135 is not less than 132, the sum exceeds 180
Part (c): angle ATB is 7°
Part (d): rejects both readings and asks for a new measurement

questions.q: The exterior angle at C of triangle ABC is (6y)° and the two opposite interior angles are (y + 20)° and (2y + 10)°. (a) Find y. (b) Find the third angle of the triangle, the one at C.

questions.q: A line XY is drawn through A parallel to BC in triangle ABC, with X on the same side of A as B and Y on the same side as C. (a) Which angles at A equal angle B and angle C, and why? (b) How does this give the angle sum?
questions.a: (a) Angle XAB = angle B and angle YAC = angle C, because they are alternate angles for the transversals AB and AC. (b) Angle XAB, angle A and angle YAC together make a straight angle of 180°, so angle B + angle A + angle C = 180°.
s: Part (a): XAB = B and YAC = C as alternate angles

questions.q: Karan says: 'An exterior angle of a triangle can have any measure between 0° and 180°.' Do you agree? Support your answer with a small and a large example.
questions.a: Yes. The exterior angle is 180° minus the interior angle at that vertex, and an interior angle can be any measure between 0° and 180°. For example, interior angle 170° gives an exterior angle of 10°, and interior angle 15° gives an exterior angle of 165° (with the other two angles making up the rest).
s: Verdict that he is right
Reason: exterior = 180° minus the interior angle, which can be any value from 0° to 180°

questions.q: Show that an exterior angle of a triangle can never be smaller than either of its two opposite interior angles.
questions.a: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. Each interior angle is more than 0°, so the sum is larger than either one of them. So the exterior angle is greater than each opposite interior angle and cannot be smaller.
s: States exterior angle = sum of the two opposite interior angles
Notes each interior angle is greater than 0°, so the sum is larger than each
Concludes the exterior angle cannot be smaller than either

questions.a: (a) ACB = 180 - 65 - 35 = 80°; ACD = 180 - 80 = 100°. (b) A + B + ACB = 180 and ACD + ACB = 180, so ACD = A + B. (c) An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of its two opposite interior angles.

Part (b): the two equations and the conclusion ACD = A + B
Part (c): states the property in words

questions.q:
A sailmaker in Kochi designs two triangular sails. In Sail P, angle A = 52° and angle B = 68°. A brochure lists Sail Q with angles 48°, 62° and 75°; the printers say the first two angles are certain. A buyer wants the sail whose largest angle is smaller, because it is more regular.
(a) Find the third angle of Sail P.
(b) Extend side BC of Sail P to D and find angle ACD.
(c) Show that the brochure for Sail Q has a misprint and find the correct third angle.
(d) Which sail should the buyer choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) 180 - 52 - 68 = 60°. (b) ACD = 180 - 60 = 120° (= 52 + 68). (c) 48 + 62 + 75 = 185, which is more than 180; the third angle should be 180 - 48 - 62 = 70°. (d) Sail P has largest angle 68° and corrected Sail Q has 70°, so the buyer should choose Sail P.
s: Part (a): angle C of Sail P is 60°
Part (b): angle ACD is 120°
Part (c): 185 is more than 180 and the correct angle is 70°
Part (d): chooses Sail P because 68 is smaller than 70

questions.q:

(b) By how much does each measured third angle differ from it?
(c) Which triangles show differences that agree with the teacher's remark about measuring error?

Part (c): T1, T2 and T3 are within 1 to 2 degrees
Part (d): remeasure T4 because 10° is too large to be a measuring error

Column II: A. Two altitudes fall outside the triangle  B. All three altitudes lie inside the triangle  C. Two altitudes are sides of the triangle  D. The crease is the altitude, perpendicular to the base
(a) Write the steps for drawing the altitude from A to BC of a triangle using a ruler and a set square. (b) Why is a set square used instead of judging the right angle by eye with a ruler alone?
questions.a: (a) Keep the ruler along BC; place the set square on the ruler with one edge of its right angle against the ruler; slide it until the upright edge touches A; draw the line from A to BC along that edge. (b) The set square gives an exact 90°; a ruler alone is not accurate for a perpendicular.
s: Part (a): ruler on the base, set square slid until the upright edge touches A, line drawn
Part (b): the set square gives a precise right angle

questions.q: In triangle TRY the angle at R is 140°. (a) Does the altitude from T fall inside or outside the triangle? (b) What must you do to the side RY before drawing it?
questions.a: (a) Outside the triangle, since the angle at R is obtuse. (b) Extend YR beyond R and draw the perpendicular from T to this extended line.
s: Part (a): outside the triangle
Part (b): extend RY beyond R and drop the perpendicular to it

questions.q: In triangle PQR the right angle is at Q. Name the altitude from P to QR and the altitude from R to PQ, and say what is special about them.
questions.a: The altitude from P to QR is PQ and the altitude from R to PQ is RQ. Each is itself a side of the triangle.
s: Names PQ and RQ as the two altitudes
States both are sides of the triangle

questions.q: A paper triangle is folded so that the base lies along itself and the crease passes through the top vertex. Justify why the crease is perpendicular to the base.
questions.a: The two parts of the base overlap exactly, so the two angles the crease makes with the base are equal. They also form a straight angle of 180°, so each is 90° and the crease is perpendicular, hence an altitude.
s: Says the two angles at the crease are equal because the base folds onto itself
Says they form a straight angle so each is 90°

questions.q: Arjun draws the 'altitude' from A to the side BC of his triangle, and a set square shows that his line makes an angle of 80° with BC. (a) Is it an altitude? (b) Explain how to correct it with a ruler and a set square.
questions.a: (a) No, an altitude must be perpendicular to BC, making 90°. (b) Put the ruler along BC, slide the set square along it until its upright edge touches A, and draw along that edge.
s: Part (a): not an altitude, since it does not make 90° with BC
Part (b): ruler on BC, set square slid until the upright edge touches A, draw along it

questions.q: Reena says: 'In a right-angled triangle the altitude from the vertex of the right angle lies inside the triangle, and so do the other two altitudes.' Is she right on both counts? Give your reasons.
questions.a: Partly right. At the right-angled vertex the perpendicular to the hypotenuse goes inside the triangle, so the first part is correct. The altitude from each of the other two vertices is the side that is perpendicular to the other side at the right angle, so those two altitudes are sides, not inside the triangle.
s: Verdict: first part right, second part wrong
Says the altitude from the right-angle vertex falls inside the triangle
Says the two sides at the right angle are themselves the other two altitudes

questions.q: In triangle TRY the angle at R is 140°. Show that the perpendicular from T cannot meet the side RY between R and Y.
questions.a: Suppose it met RY at D between R and Y. Then triangle TRD would have angle D = 90° and angle R = 140°, which together make 230°, more than 180°. That cannot happen, so D lies beyond R on the extended side.
s: Supposes the foot D is between R and Y
Finds angles 90 and 140 in triangle TRD adding to 230°
Concludes this is impossible by the angle sum so the foot is outside

questions.q: Describe an acute-angled triangle by its three angles and say where all three altitudes lie. Then change the angles, keeping the sum 180°, so that two altitudes fall outside, and say what kind of triangle you made.
questions.a: Acute: 60°, 70°, 50°; all three altitudes lie inside the triangle. Changed: 110°, 35°, 35°; the angle 110° is obtuse, so the altitudes from the two acute vertices fall outside on extended sides. The triangle is obtuse-angled.
s: An acute set adding to 180° with all altitudes inside
An obtuse set adding to 180°
Says the two altitudes from the acute vertices fall outside and names it obtuse-angled

questions.q: Write the steps to construct triangle LMN with MN = 5 cm, LM = 6 cm and angle M = 130°, and then the altitude from L to MN.
questions.a: Draw MN = 5 cm. At M make an angle of 130° and mark L on the arm with ML = 6 cm. Join LN. Extend NM beyond M. Place a ruler along the extended line, slide the set square till its upright edge touches L, and draw the perpendicular from L to the extended line.
s: Draws MN = 5 cm
Makes 130° at M and marks L with ML = 6 cm
Joins LN
Extends NM beyond M
Draws the perpendicular from L to the extended line with a set square

questions.q: Construct triangle PQR with QR = 6 cm, PQ = 7 cm and PR = 4 cm, and the altitude from P to QR. (a) Write the construction steps for the triangle. (b) Name the triangle by its sides. (c) Write the steps for the altitude and name its foot D.
questions.a: (a) Draw QR = 6 cm; from Q draw an arc of radius 7 cm and from R an arc of radius 4 cm; they cross at P; join PQ and PR. (b) Scalene, since 7, 6 and 4 are all different. (c) With the ruler along QR, slide the set square till its upright edge touches P and draw the perpendicular from P to QR, meeting it at D.
s: Part (a): base QR, arcs of 7 cm from Q and 4 cm from R, joins P
Part (b): scalene with three different sides
Part (c): set square slid to P and the perpendicular drawn to meet QR at D

questions.q:
For the annual-day decoration, Mrs Devi cuts triangular flags. To find the height of flag ABC she folds the paper so that the side BC lies along itself, with the crease passing through A and meeting BC at D. Flag PQR has a right angle at Q. Flag XYZ has angle Y = 118°. With a set square, an altitude that lies inside a flag takes her 1 minute to draw and measure, but one that needs a side extended takes 2 minutes. She has only 4 minutes to record heights on flag XYZ.
(a) What is the crease AD called, and what angle does it make with BC?
(b) In flag PQR, does the altitude from Q to PR lie inside the flag or along a side?
(c) For flag XYZ, how many altitudes need a side extended?
(d) Which heights of flag XYZ can she record in 4 minutes, and can she record all three? Show the times.
questions.a: (a) AD is an altitude and it makes 90° with BC. (b) Inside the flag, since PR is a side that the perpendicular from Q meets at a point of PR. (c) Two: the altitudes from X and Z need a side extended because the angle at Y is obtuse. (d) The altitude from Y (inside) takes 1 minute, each of the other two takes 2 minutes. All three would take 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 minutes, more than 4; she can record the height from Y and one of the others (1 + 2 = 3 minutes), but not all three.
s: Part (a): altitude, 90°
Part (b): inside the flag
Part (c): two altitudes need a side extended
Part (d): 5 minutes for all three exceeds 4; she can do Y plus one other in 3 minutes

questions.q:
A panchayat has three triangular plots. Plot 1 has angles 55°, 60° and 65°. Plot 2 has angles 90°, 40° and 50°. Plot 3 has angles 140°, 25° and 15° at its corners R, T and Y respectively. In each plot a well must be dug at the foot of a perpendicular from a corner to the opposite boundary, and the panchayat rule says the foot must lie on the plot's own boundary. For Plot 3, the first choice is the foot of the perpendicular from R to the side TY (an 8 m pipe). The second choice is the foot of the perpendicular from T to the line RY, which needs a 14 m pipe and also a strip of the neighbour's land costing ₹3,000. Pipe costs ₹150 per metre.
(a) In which plot are two of the altitudes sides of the plot?
(b) In Plot 3, how many altitudes have their foot outside the plot?
(c) Why does the second choice's foot lie outside the plot?
(d) Find the total cost of each choice and say which the panchayat can accept, with the reason.
questions.a: (a) Plot 2, which has a right angle. (b) Two, those from T and Y. (c) Because the angle at R is 140°, which is obtuse, the perpendicular from T meets the line RY beyond R, outside the plot. (d) The foot of the perpendicular from R to TY costs 8 x 150 = ₹1,200. The foot of the perpendicular from T to RY costs 3,000 + 14 x 150 = ₹5,100. The first is both cheaper and the only one whose foot lies on the boundary, so the panchayat can accept only the perpendicular from R to TY.
s: Part (a): Plot 2
Part (b): two altitudes, from T and Y
Part (c): the foot is beyond R on the extended line since the angle at R is obtuse
Part (d): costs ₹1,200 and ₹5,100 and accepts the R-to-TY well as cheaper and on the boundary

questions.q: Classified by the lengths of its sides, a triangle with sides 8 cm, 9 cm and 10 cm is
questions.a: scalene

questions.q: An acute-angled triangle is defined as one in which
questions.a: all three angles are acute
o: at least one angle is acute

questions.q: A triangle has angles 100°, 50° and 30°. By its angles it is
questions.a: obtuse-angled
o: acute-angled, since two angles are acute

questions.q: A triangular floor tile has three sides of 13 cm each and each of its angles measures 60°. Which pair of names fits it?
questions.a: equilateral and acute-angled

questions.q: A triangular park has sides 40 m, 50 m and 80 m and its largest angle measures 125°. Which pair of names fits it?
questions.a: scalene and obtuse-angled

questions.q:
Read the statements about types of triangles.
Statement 1: A triangle can have two obtuse angles if its sides are long enough.
Statement 2: An acute-angled triangle has exactly one acute angle.
Statement 3: A scalene triangle has all three sides of different lengths.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A triangle with sides 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm is isosceles.
Reason (R): Triangles are also classified by their angles as acute-angled, right-angled or obtuse-angled.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each description in Column I with the correct description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Sides 3.5 cm, 3.5 cm, 3.5 cm  2. Sides 4 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm  3. Sides 4 cm, 5 cm, 6 cm  4. Angles 110°, 40°, 30°
Column II: A. All three sides different  B. Exactly two sides equal  C. One angle greater than 90°  D. All three sides equal

(a) Classify by the lengths of their sides: a triangle with sides 6 cm, 6 cm, 9 cm and a triangle with sides 5 cm, 7 cm, 9 cm. (b) Classify by angles: a triangle with angles 54, 63, 63° and one with angles 90, 35, 55°.
questions.a: (a) 6, 6, 9 is isosceles; 5, 7, 9 is scalene. (b) 54, 63, 63° is acute-angled (all angles acute); 90, 35, 55° is right-angled.
s: Part (a): isosceles and scalene
Part (b): acute-angled and right-angled

questions.q: Two angles of a triangle are 38° and 52°. (a) Find the third angle. (b) Name the triangle by its angles.
questions.a: (a) 180 - 38 - 52 = 90°. (b) It has a right angle, so it is right-angled.
s: Part (a): the third angle is 90°
Part (b): right-angled

questions.q: Why is 'a triangle with one acute angle' not a correct definition of an acute-angled triangle? Give an example.
questions.a: Right-angled and obtuse-angled triangles also have acute angles; for example a triangle with angles 90, 50 and 40° has acute angles but is not acute-angled. An acute-angled triangle needs all three angles acute.
s: Says triangles of other types also have an acute angle, with an example
States all three angles must be acute

questions.q: Meena constructs triangle ABC with AB = 3 cm, AC = 4 cm and angle A = 90°, and measures BC as 5 cm. (a) Name the triangle by its sides. (b) Name it by its angles.
questions.a: (a) The sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm are all different, so it is scalene. (b) It has a right angle at A, so it is right-angled.
s: Part (a): scalene because the three sides differ
Part (b): right-angled

questions.q: Construct (describe) a triangle with AB = AC = 4 cm and angle A = 110°. (a) Give the steps. (b) Name it by its sides and by its angles, with the reason.
questions.a: (a) Draw AB = 4 cm, make 110° at A and mark C on the arm with AC = 4 cm; join BC. (b) Isosceles by sides (AB = AC); obtuse-angled because the angle A = 110° is more than 90°.
s: Part (a): base, 110° at A, C at 4 cm, join BC
Part (b): isosceles by sides and obtuse-angled because of the 110 degree angle

questions.q: Nisha says: 'A triangle can have two right angles, because 90° + 90° = 180° and the third angle can be a very small one.' Do you agree? Use the angle sum to explain.
questions.a: No. Two right angles already add to 180°, so the third angle would be 0°, which is no angle at all. The three angles must add to 180° with each positive, so a triangle has at most one right angle.
s: Verdict that Nisha is wrong
Shows 90° + 90° = 180° leaves 0° for the third angle
Concludes at most one angle can be a right angle

questions.q: Show that no triangle can be both right-angled and obtuse-angled.
questions.a: A right angle is 90° and an obtuse angle is more than 90°, so together they add to more than 180°, even before adding the third angle. The angles of a triangle add to exactly 180°, so this cannot happen.
s: States right angle is 90° and obtuse is more than 90°
Adds them to get more than 180°
Contradicts the angle sum 180°

questions.q: Write the three angles of (i) an obtuse-angled triangle, (ii) an acute-angled triangle and (iii) a right-angled triangle, and check each set adds up correctly.
questions.a: (i) 110, 40, 30°: sum 180, one angle above 90. (ii) 70, 60, 50°: sum 180, all below 90. (iii) 90, 45, 45°: sum 180, one angle of 90.
s: Obtuse set with sum 180 and one angle above 90
Acute set with sum 180 and all angles below 90
Right set with sum 180 and one angle of 90

questions.q: Three triangles are given. Triangle 1 has angles 35°, 65° and x. Triangle 2 has angles 28°, 62° and y. Triangle 3 has angles 40°, 30° and z. (a) Find x, y and z. (b) Name each triangle by its angles. (c) Which of them has two altitudes that are its own sides?
questions.a: (a) x = 180 - 35 - 65 = 80; y = 180 - 28 - 62 = 90; z = 180 - 40 - 30 = 110°. (b) Triangle 1 is acute-angled, triangle 2 is right-angled, triangle 3 is obtuse-angled. (c) Triangle 2, because it has a right angle.
s: Part (b): acute, right and obtuse
Part (c): triangle 2, the right-angled one

questions.q: Explore which kinds of triangles exist. (a) Describe a construction of an isosceles right-angled triangle with equal sides of 4.5 cm. (b) Describe a construction of an isosceles obtuse-angled triangle with equal sides of 3.5 cm and the angle between them 130°. (c) An equilateral triangle of side 5.5 cm is constructed with a compass and each angle is measured as 60°. By its angles, what kind of triangle is it?
questions.a: (a) Draw AB = 4.5 cm, make 90° at B and mark C with BC = 4.5 cm; join AC. (b) Draw AB = 3.5 cm, make 130° at A, mark C with AC = 3.5 cm and join BC. (c) Every angle is less than 90°, so it is acute-angled.
s: Part (a): AB = BC = 4.5 cm with 90° at B
Part (b): AB = AC = 3.5 cm with 130° at A
Part (c): acute-angled

questions.q:
Mr Iqbal's art class cuts five triangular cards and measures two angles of each. Card P has sides 10 cm, 10 cm, 10 cm and angles 60° and 60°. Card Q has sides 9 cm, 9 cm, 14 cm and angles 39° and 39°. Card R has sides 8 cm, 10 cm, 12 cm and angles 41.4° and 55.8°. Card S has sides 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm and angles 36.9° and 53.1°. Card T has sides 7 cm, 8 cm, 9 cm and angles 48.2° and 58.4°.
(a) Classify each card by its sides.
(b) Find the third angle of each card and classify each card by its angles.
(c) Which card has two altitudes that are its own sides?
(d) For a display the teacher wants a card that is both acute-angled and scalene, with a border costing ₹3 per cm of perimeter. Which card should she pick, and what is the border cost?
questions.a: (a) P equilateral, Q isosceles, R scalene, S scalene, T scalene. (b) Third angles: P 60°, Q 102°, R 82.8°, S 90°, T 73.4°; so P acute, Q obtuse, R acute, S right, T acute. (c) Card S. (d) The acute scalene cards are R (perimeter 30 cm, border ₹90) and T (perimeter 24 cm, border ₹72); pick T for ₹72.
s: Part (a): equilateral, isosceles, scalene, scalene, scalene
Part (b): third angles 60, 102, 82.8, 90, 73.4 and acute, obtuse, acute, right, acute
Part (c): Card S, the right-angled one
Part (d): chooses T with border ₹72 against ₹90 for R

questions.q:
A surveyor's register lists the corner angles of four plots. Plot A: 48, 67, 65°. Plot B: 90, 28, 62°. Plot C: 22, 31, 127°. Plot D: 55, 60, 75°. The clerk suspects that one entry was typed wrongly.
(a) Which plot's entry cannot be right, and what is its angle sum?
(b) Classify plots A, B and C by their angles.
(c) If the angles 60 and 75 for Plot D are correct, what should the first angle be, and what kind of triangle is Plot D then?
(d) Should the clerk send the surveyor to re-measure all four plots or only some? Give your decision with the reason.
questions.a: (a) Plot D: 55 + 60 + 75 = 190, not 180°. (b) A acute-angled, B right-angled, C obtuse-angled. (c) 180 - 60 - 75 = 45°; Plot D is then acute-angled. (d) Only Plot D needs re-measuring: A, B and C each add up to 180°, so they pass the angle sum check, while D fails it.
s: Part (a): Plot D with sum 190
Part (b): acute, right, obtuse
Part (c): 45° and acute-angled
Part (d): re-measure only D because the others add up to 180
